A Simple, and Quick, Guide to Reading Your Tires

This is a great article. I recently bought motorcycle tires online. A local mechanic told me I should be careful be he's heard stories of people getting old tires online. When they were delivered, I was pleased to see my new tires had been made earlier that month.

Reading your tires is an important life skill.

Age of tires are such a touchy topic for some people and there are tons of disagreements on them. Personally, I wouldn't think twice of running tires that are "new" and five years old. Unless they were stored in horrible conditions, they're going to be fine. Hell, the MTRs I'm running on my truck right now are around 8-9 years old. I look at them every day and inspect them, and they're wearing and running fine. I wouldn't suggest this to everyone, though. I've been around the tire business my whole life and can recognize possible issues before they become issues. But I digress.

It's great that you got fresh tires. And, on a bike, I would be more specific about the age of my tires. But people who get worried about tires that are a year or two old have nothing to worry about.

I also don't feel that buying used tires are a problem. Some people do. If it's a shady business selling used tires, stay away. If it's a well known and respected business in the area, feel safe. A lot of people cannot afford brand new tires and, if you're buying used from a respect dealer, there should be nothing to worry about. They're not going to mount dry-rotted or patched up tires for you.

Most big tire companies ( Continental, Goodyear, Firestone) agree that a tires life span is about 10 years. If you buy a five year old tire for your vehicle, you're going to wear it out prior to that ten-year life span.

Great response. I'd upvoat you twice if I could.

Key point in most tire discussion is inspection. Keep an eye on your tires. Recognize changes when they occur and replace them as needed.

What's your message to those who don't think running sounds particularly fun?

Honestly, that's up to you. I know a lot of people who don't necessarily like it, but they like to think about what they're doing for themselves to keep healthy. As /u/fljared mentioned, doing a race could be very helpful, especially for those who are very competitive. It give you a goal to strive for and if you're anything like me, when you're in a race, your competitiveness comes out and you just try to pass and beat everyone in front of you. No one likes running when they first do it. You just have to buck up and try it. Eventually your body will get used to it and you'll be setting personal records as time goes on. Nothing feels better than when you set a new PR. It takes approximately two weeks for your body to get into shape and used to what you're doing to it. Just give it time and you'll be running miles in no time.

Excellent advice and encouragement! Also, to those who say "I only run when my activity of choice involves running!"

Imagine how much better at that activity you would be if you ran on off-days!

But yes OP...running is good.

There are those that go out and buy the most expensive shoe and all that, but you really don't need to. When they come out with these new version of the shoes, not much is really changing. Sure there are some slight updates, but nothing that will significantly enhance your experience. I for example, like to keep my running shoe spending as low as possible. I get the earliest edition of shoes I can because it's cheaper (I bought the Brooks Ghost 5 when the Ghost 7 came out).

Everything else in running is really a commodity. You don't really need special shirts, shoes (given you don't require it for a physical impairment), etc. As a runner you can go out and run anywhere at any time.
